Using the application

Open it from the link at the top of this page. Everything is driven from the control bar across the top and from the three map titles.

ControlWhat it does
ShowThree tick boxes, one per product. Untick one to take its map off the screen.
LevelSwitches the legend between the seven UNCCD reporting classes, each product’s own general classes, and its full class list — the last of these exists for GLAD only.
YearNearest to 2023, 2019, 2015 or 2000. Each map moves to the nearest date that product actually has, which is not always the one selected.
RegionThe whole country, an oblast, or a district. Every percentage under the maps is a share of whatever is selected here.
Tick box on a map titleHides that one product without changing the others.
Slider on a map titleFades the classification against the satellite image underneath — the quickest way to check a class against what is on the ground.
The three mapsLinked. Pan or zoom one and the other two follow.
Legend under each mapThe product’s class list, with each class’s share of the selected region beside it.

Looking at the disaggregated classes of the selected land cover products

All three products map the same country in the same seven reporting classes. They still disagree, sometimes by a lot. The disagreement is not error: each product draws the line between classes in a different place.

Three examples in different regions

Kostanay

How much of the region is cropland?

52.5%ESA CCI
53.7%GLC_FCS30D
27.1%GLAD GLCLU

The big cropland block in the north is solid for two products and broken up for the third. Nothing on the ground changed between the three pictures.

East Kazakhstan

How much of the region is tree covered?

24.2%ESA CCI
40.1%GLC_FCS30D
17.8%GLAD GLCLU

Forest in the Altai differs by more than a factor of two between the highest and the lowest.

Nur-Sultan

How much of the city area is cropland?

32.8%ESA CCI
51.9%GLC_FCS30D
3.7%GLAD GLCLU

The built-up core agrees in all three. What surrounds it does not.

The same view, two dates

The four examples above change the product. This pair changes the year instead, over the same view. All three products lose water in the same place.

They agree the water has gone. They do not agree on what replaced it, and that is what decides whether the change is counted as degradation.

Why any of this matters. Run the same degradation calculation on Kostanay with each product and the answer is 0.59% with ESA CCI, 2.86% with GLAD GLCLU and 5.93% with GLC_FCS30D. Ten times larger from one end to the other, over the same region and the same period. Choosing the product is a reporting decision, not a technical detail.

Why the detailed classes matter

The seven reporting classes are a summary. Underneath each one the product keeps its own detailed classes, and that is where the answers to most partner questions live. Two of them are worth keeping visible when the seven are agreed.

Shrubland is reported inside Grassland. If shrubs spread into pasture, or are cleared and lost, the Grassland total barely moves — the process does not appear in the reported number at all.

Irrigated cropland is reported inside Cropland. If irrigation fails and the land returns to rainfed farming or to bare ground, Cropland can stay almost unchanged, while what happened on the ground is exactly the kind of change the Convention exists to track.

What this looks like in Kyzylorda

Kyzylorda is a good place to see it. The region sits on the Syr Darya: irrigation is the reason the cropland exists, and shrub cover is a large part of what the seven classes simply call grassland.

If a partner asks how much of our pasture is shrub. ESA CCI answers 23.6% of the region and GLC_FCS30D 31.2%, each as a named Shrubland line inside Grassland. GLAD has no such line: its grassland is a single block of 64.5% labelled simply “semi-arid, 11–75% vegetation cover”. Two products can answer the question and one cannot.

If a partner asks how much of our cropland depends on irrigation. In Kyzylorda almost all of it does: ESA CCI puts 8.6 of its 8.8% of cropland in “irrigated or post-flooding”, GLC_FCS30D 8.0 of 8.2% in “irrigated cropland”. GLAD reports 1.2% cropland in total, in one undivided class, and cannot say how much of it is irrigated.

Both classes exist in ESA CCI and in GLC_FCS30D. Neither exists in GLAD GLCLU. So the choice of product decides, before any analysis is run, whether Kazakhstan can answer either question — and that is a decision for the workshop, not for later.

Why GLAD cannot provide them

ESA CCI and GLC_FCS30D name their classes: shrubland, irrigated cropland, swamp. GLAD does not name anything. Its classes are two measurements — how much low vegetation covers the ground, and how tall the trees are.

What to decide in the workshop

  • Which product. The ordering of the three is consistent across regions, so the choice moves the reported figure in a predictable direction. It should be a decision on the record, with a reason.
  • Whether seven classes are enough. Mongolia reported into the seven platform classes while working internally with twelve. If Kazakhstan wants shrubland or irrigated cropland separated, that decision has to come before the analysis — and it rules out GLAD GLCLU.
  • What each change means. Agreeing the classes is only half of it. The transition matrix decides which changes count as degradation, and that is a second, separate choice.
